notes.meaning: Jericho barred its gates tightly because the people were terrified of the advancing Israelites. No one could enter or leave the heavily guarded fortress. The inhabitants chose to rely on their thick stone walls and stubbornly set themselves against God instead of seeking peace.

The Lord told Joshua that Jericho was already given into his hands, along with its king and brave fighters. God spoke of this victory as already accomplished because His promises never fail. Even though the defenders were skilled in war, God assured Joshua of an easy and total triumph.

God gave Joshua an unusual battle plan that used no human weapons or siege towers. The soldiers were to march around the city once a day for six days, accompanied by seven priests blowing ram's-horn trumpets before the ark of the Lord. On the seventh day, they would circle seven times, blow a long blast, and shout, causing the wall to collapse so the soldiers could charge straight inside. The ark was a sacred chest symbolizing God's holy presence, showing that this victory would come by His power alone.

Joshua immediately obeyed God's instructions without hesitation or debate. He called the priests to carry the holy ark and told seven of them to carry the trumpets ahead of it. He then directed the armed soldiers to march out in front to protect the procession.

The people moved out in orderly ranks exactly as they had been directed. Armed men led the way, the priests continually sounded their horns before the ark, and a rear guard followed behind the sacred chest. The continuous horn blasts reminded Israel of God's presence and warned Jericho of coming judgment.

Joshua strictly commanded the soldiers to maintain complete silence while marching. They were not to utter a word or raise a battle cry until the appointed day and moment. This quietness tested their patience, teaching them to listen to God's horn blasts and wait for His timing.

The priests carried the ark around the walls of Jericho once on the first day. When the circuit was finished, the army returned to their camp and spent the night there. Nothing seemed to change on the walls, requiring the people to rest in quiet faith.

Joshua rose early the next morning, and the priests and soldiers repeated the exact same quiet march. They circled the city once each day for six days in a row and then returned to camp. This steady routine proved Israel's willingness to obey God step by step, even when no immediate results could be seen.

On the seventh day, the Israelites got up at dawn to circle the city seven times. This was the only day on which they made multiple trips around the walls, requiring extra energy and endurance. The number seven highlighted that God's complete and perfect work of judgment had arrived.

At the end of the seventh circuit, the priests blew a long horn blast, and Joshua commanded the people to shout. He declared with certainty that the Lord had already given them the city. Their mighty shout was a bold cry of faith that claimed the victory before the walls had even moved.

Joshua announced that Jericho was devoted to the Lord for destruction, meaning everything inside was set apart as an offering to God's justice and could not be kept as personal loot. Only Rahab and the family inside her house were spared because she had safely hidden the Israelite messengers. All gold, silver, bronze, and iron were set apart for the Lord's sanctuary, and Joshua warned that taking any devoted thing would bring disaster upon the entire camp.

When the horns blew, the people raised a massive shout, and the city walls fell flat to the ground. Every soldier charged directly forward into the city from wherever he stood without meeting any barrier. God's miraculous power brought down the fortifications in an instant, giving His people the victory.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars argue that the walls fell through natural causes, such as an earthquake or military undermining, rather than a direct miracle.

notes.meaning: The soldiers put everyone in the city to death with the sword, including men, women, young, old, and livestock. God acted as the righteous Judge against a culture whose severe wickedness had reached its full measure over hundreds of years. Israel carried out this difficult order not out of personal malice, but as the appointed instruments of God's holy justice.

Joshua sent the two original spies into Rahab's house to bring out her and her entire family, honoring the solemn oath they had sworn to her. The spies led her parents, brothers, and relatives to safety outside the Israelite camp. They stayed outside the camp for a time to be cleansed from foreign pagan ways before joining God's people.

The Israelites set fire to Jericho and burned the entire city with everything in it. They preserved only the metals that could survive fire, placing the silver, gold, bronze, and iron into the tabernacle's treasury. This confirmed that the wealth of the first conquered city belonged entirely to God as firstfruits.

Joshua kept Rahab and her family safe because she had shown faith by protecting the messengers. She became a permanent member of Israel, and her descendants continued to live among God's people. Her salvation shows that God graciously receives anyone who turns to Him in faith, no matter their past.

Joshua placed a solemn curse on anyone who would ever attempt to rebuild Jericho as a fortified city. He declared that the builder would lose his firstborn son when laying its foundations and his youngest child when hanging its gates. The ruins were intended to remain as a lasting reminder of God's holy power and judgment against sin.

The Lord stayed with Joshua, guiding and prospering his work just as He had promised. Joshua's reputation and renown quickly spread across the entire land of Canaan. True greatness comes from having the clear presence and blessing of God upon one's life.
